body: Results for the experiments based on MS values 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 for the second extended model named:Socially enabled and Monopolized Toy Trader Model (SocMonoToyModel), in terms of different parameters are presented in Fig. 4C---for gini co-efficient, Fig. 5C---for wealth distribution, Fig. 6C---for wealth gap, Fig. 7C---for price and number of trades, and Fig. 4C---for poverty. Gini coefficient: Since, SocToyModel added monopoly to the model, which has already social influence incorporated, it should have further impact on the results. To endorse this claim, the gini coefficient values for the SocToyModel were found greater than the responses for SocToyModel as illustrated in Fig. 4C in comparison with the corresponding results presented in Fig. 4B---whose responses were greater than the toy trader model responses presented earlier in Fig. 4A. However, gini coefficient got stabilized much earlier than the responses obtained for the SocToyModel. For example, the results for MS values 4 and 8 were around 0.6 (see Fig. 4C(c)), which is higher than SocToyModel responses presented in Fig. 4B(c)). Fig. 4C(e) and B(e) both have almost the same results for an MS value 16 in both the extensions.

Wealth gap for SocToyModel (given in Fig. 6C(a)) was huge and happened quickly in a similar fashion observed earlier for SocToyModel (given in Fig. 6B(a)) against an MS value 1. Fig. 6C(c) has also a very clear and stable wider division between top-20% and bottom-80% population than the same for SocToyModel presented in Fig. 6B(c). The results for bigger values of MS (8 and 16), presented in Fig 6C(d)–(e), have also not only a wider but more clear and stable division, than the results for the same scenarios of SocToyModel presented in Fig 6B(d)–(e). Surprisingly, the wealth gap in both the models was minimum for MS value 2. Prices and trades: Experimental results regarding the prices of toys and the number of trades for SocMonoToyModel are presented in Fig. 7C for all the cases based on 5 different MS values. Comparing these results with the corresponding results of SocToyModel (presented in Fig. 7B), it is learnt that prices increase in SocMonoToyModel was lower for the MS values of 4, 8, and 16. However, these are still not that significant. The poverty for the remaining cases remained 0, exactly the same as SocToyModel. It means that more market visibility help the traders to earn money and, thus, take them out of poverty. When the overall results of the SocMonoToyModel are compared with the responses obtained for SocToyModel, it is revealed that both have similar response but the former had even worst response in terms of wealth distribution, wealth gap and poverty. 5 Conclusion and Future Directions This work first explored the toy trader model, which, contrary to the common sense, turned out to be unfair in terms of wealth gap and poverty. The model was run for different values of Market Sight. It was learnt that wealth disparity index (gini coefficient) is positively influenced by the increase in MS value. The distribution of wealth though does not have a definite pattern, however, generally, the increase in MS value generates more rich people. The rational was to find the impact of market visibility and monopoly on wealth distribution and poverty. Simulation results of both the extended models revealed that they not only widened the rich-poor divide but also increased the poverty.
